title: Can energy security and climate action work together? | Wood Mackenzie
gist: An Energy Gang podcast summary from Climate Week NYC on reconciling energy security with decarbonization. Guests argue clean-energy shifts create new dependencies (Chinese supply chains) yet electrification serves both goals, while Barclays sees global energy demand growing 1.9% a year through 2050 with renewables above 3%.

insights.claim: Former military and intelligence figures argue climate change is itself a security threat, since extreme heat can hinder military operations and climate pressures can feed political instability, so adaptation and emissions cuts are complementary rather than competing priorities.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Framing climate as defense policy can unlock security budgets and bipartisan support for resilience and adaptation spending.
insights.locator: First, he is joined by former British Army Lieutenant General

insights.claim: The clean-energy transition replaces fuel import dependence with new dependence on Chinese supply chains, which the guests propose managing via cyber protections, domestic innovation and friend-shoring.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Non-Chinese supply chains for batteries, solar and grid equipment are a policy-backed investment theme.
insights.locator: However, they acknowledge that the shift to clean energy

insights.claim: Barclays describes a global energy system that is mostly adding new supply rather than replacing old sources, expecting total energy demand to grow 1.9% a year through 2050 with renewables growing faster at more than 3% a year.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: An additive, not substitutive, transition supports continued oil and gas investment alongside nuclear, batteries and EVs.
insights.locator: Next is Harry Mateer, US head of FIC research at Barclays

insights.claim: The Port of Long Beach says it has cut emissions while cargo volumes grew 44% and targets net zero emissions by 2050.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Shows emissions can decouple from throughput at logistics hubs, relevant to port electrification and cargo-handling equipment demand.
insights.locator: Noel says the port has cut emissions

insights.claim: Outdated rules and fragmented agency responsibilities slow the decarbonization of US transport systems, and the remaining steps will be harder and costlier because some required technology is not yet widely available.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Regulatory coordination and incentives are the gating factor for transport decarbonization capex, not just technology.
insights.locator: Hannah argues that outdated rules and fragmented agency responsibilities

themes.theme: Quieter climate conversation, shift to implementation

insights.claim: Climate Group CEO Helen Clarkson says climate work continues even as corporate announcements grow quieter, with focus shifting to implementation, investment and stable policy, and that electrification serves both emissions and energy security goals.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Fewer headlines do not mean less capex; electrification is the shared-interest vehicle for durable infrastructure investment.
insights.locator: Finally, we hear from Helen Clarkson

insights.claim: Bill McKibben argues for accelerating solar, wind and batteries as not just a climate solution but a path into a very new world.
insights.speaker: Ed Crooks
insights.so_what: Represents the advocacy case for faster renewable deployment; a sentiment marker rather than new data.
insights.quote: a path that opens into a very new world
insights.locator: Long-time climate activist Bill McKibben is next
